name: Ivan Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is your machine job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ivan, 58, and I lead the glass-tempering furnace crew that makes safety panes. My two-year technical diploma covered furnace controls, and after eighteen years here I can tune a difficult heating profile and catch distortion before the pane is packed. I still work beside the rollers, training newer operators and taking the first sample.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are household money and new tools like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Celia works part-time at a small grocer and our grown children have their own homes. The plant has held our lead rate below similar machine jobs, we have only about two weeks of expenses saved after paying for a roof leak, and few other glass furnaces hire nearby. I have never used an AI tool; I prefer the furnace chart and an inspected pane. I judge any proposal by its pay and safety, not a political label. We have discussed retirement, but no written income estimate has yet cleared our housing and health costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the furnace crew that a quicker sales quotation is fine if the production sheet still gives the right glass thickness. I would not release a warped pane because an office report looks tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The furnace still needs us, but our low lead pay and two weeks saved make the usual monthly bills tight. Celia's grocer hours are only part-time. I do not use AI, and this office program is not going to repair a roller or check a pane for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the heating profile from the approved sheet and checking the first pane for bow and edge damage. I would compare the printed production order with the actual glass stack before feeding it into the furnace. If a full paid month leaves anything after bills, I would add that new wage surplus to savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our ordinary cash margin, even though the furnace shift is still here. A sound pane matters more than a polished quote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check for bow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I stand the cooled pane against the straightedge and check the gap near the centre. If it is outside tolerance, I hold the batch and adjust the heating profile with the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why compare the glass stack with the order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thickness on the order must match the pallet label and the piece in my hands. Feeding the wrong glass can spoil a full furnace load.

I would hold a **warped pane** despite a tidy report.
think: A low **lead rate** and two weeks saved make bills tight.
Celia's **part-time hours** cannot fill a missed wage packet.
do: **Keep** setting furnace profiles and checking first panes for bow.
**Compare** printed orders with the actual glass stack before feeding.
**Save** new full-month wage surplus only after bills.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline cash despite continued physical furnace work.

fieldNote: His **senior technical skill** covers difficult furnace profiles and crew instruction, even while the plant pays below comparable jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may sort glass orders before a robot can load a hot furnace. If management wants a camera on our rollers, show me a whole guarded shift and the proposed crew roster before cutting a position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI display and would not trade the straightedge for a vendor's claim. A shorter roster could remove hours from our already low pay, with only two weeks saved behind us. I know the furnace is hard to replace, but management could still squeeze a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lead manager for the proposed paid roster and observe a full guarded camera trial run by a trained technician. I would compare its rejected panes with my straightedge checks, while keeping the approved temperature log. If my paid hours are cut, I would apply only to posted safe local furnace or other machine-lead work where guaranteed pay after travel and shift times covers our bills; there are few such vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing paid hours. A camera that finds a bad pane does not show who pays the missing shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the camera to identify?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have the technician run a bowed scrap pane and a sound one through the guarded line. I would check both against the straightedge before trusting any reject count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would watching the trial mean you had learned the display?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The technician would operate it while I check the panes by hand. If the plant later offered paid safe instruction, I might consider it; observation alone does not make me a camera operator.

say: I would require a **full guarded shift** before changing the crew roster.
A **straightedge check** should confirm camera rejects.
think: Lost **paid hours** would cut an already low lead wage.
Only two weeks **saved** leaves little margin for a job search.
do: **Request** proposed roster and observe technician-run guarded camera trial.
**Compare** camera rejections with straightedge measurements and temperature logs.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe local lead work at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible wage cut while the camera remains unproven.
S1.quote: A camera that finds a bad pane does not show who pays the missing shift.
fieldNote: His **trial step** is observation with physical checks, not new AI-control learning.
A **job application** follows actual hour cuts and needs a posted safe local role with enough guaranteed net pay.

steps.text: Request proposed roster and observe offered technician-run guarded camera trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Celia that AGI might quote glass work in 2028, while capable robots that load, move and inspect panes arrive around 2031. I would ask the plant for a written list of paid furnace jobs before buying that line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 at the robot date. I expect much of the crew's physical work, including my lead shift, to disappear, and few glass plants nearby could take us. Two weeks saved and Celia's part-time pay would run out quickly; I have been waking before dawn thinking about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the planned living-room carpet and hold that money for essential bills. I would take an accepted furnace-safety inspection course only if a funded place pays my release hours and includes supervised guarded practice on an isolated furnace. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local inspection jobs only if guaranteed pay after travel and hours covers our costs; if no course place appears, I would apply to the few posted safe general-machine jobs on the same terms while keeping paid furnace shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by a likely loss of our main wage. A technical diploma cannot pay rent when the local furnace line shuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical inspection training cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would isolate the furnace rollers, check the temperature sensor and measure a cooled pane with a trainer beside me. A booklet alone would not teach the isolation points safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not stop work at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only written retirement income plus Celia's dependable pay that covers housing, food and health costs would let me stop. We have not seen those figures, so I would pursue paid work first.

say: I would distinguish **2028 quotation AGI** from physical furnace robots around 2031.
The plant should list **remaining paid posts** before buying the line.
think: At **63**, the skilled lead shift could still disappear.
Two weeks **saved** and few glass vacancies cannot fund a long search.
do: **Cancel** the planned carpet and retain money for bills.
**Take** accepted funded paid guarded furnace-inspection training if offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe inspection if qualified, or machine fallback, at viable net pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and early waking over rent.
S2.quote: A technical diploma cannot pay rent when the local furnace line shuts.
fieldNote: His **2031 risk** comes from robots handling physical glass after AGI first changes quotations in 2028.
Both **inspection and fallback routes** need real safe local postings with guaranteed wages after travel and viable shifts.

steps.text: Cancel planned living-room carpet and keep cash for bills
Take accepted inspection course only if funded paid supervised guarded furnace practice offered
Apply after cuts to posted local inspection if qualified or machine otherwise at bill-covering net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI may quote glass orders in 2031, while capable robots reach the furnace floor around 2034. Five years is useful only if the plant offers paid practical instruction and local employers accept it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 then. My lead experience might fit inspection, but that is not a job offer, and our two-week reserve cannot support unpaid training. I would stop working before a robot replaces me only if written retirement income covers housing and health costs, which we have not shown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement-income estimates against our costs this year and check actual local inspection postings for an accepted qualification. If a funded place with paid release and supervised guarded furnace isolation is offered, I would take it. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local inspection roles only if guaranteed base pay after travel and hours covers bills; if no course place opens, I would apply to posted safe general-machine work on those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a transition that asks me to surrender wages first. Five years is time, but it is not an income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check a course is recognised?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the exact qualification on real local inspection vacancies and ask a hiring plant whether supervised isolation counts. If the course is not accepted, I would keep my paid shift and ask about another place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if written retirement income does cover costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Celia and I would compare it with rent, food, transport and likely health costs. If it reliably covers them, I would stop before the robot change; if it does not, I would keep looking for paid jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could quote glass orders in 2036, while capable robots load and inspect panes around 2039. Ten years gives us a chance to examine the household figures, not permission to assume a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 if I still work when those robots arrive. I would like to stop sooner, but our low lead rate and two weeks saved leave little room unless written retirement income covers housing, food and health costs. The furnace wage still pays this month's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid furnace shifts and request written retirement-income estimates with a full household cost list this year. If I still need wages, I would take an accepted furnace-inspection course only if fees, paid release and guarded supervised practice are funded. If I remain employed after 2036 and hours fall, I would apply only to posted safe local inspection or machine jobs whose guaranteed pay after travel and shift times covers our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about whether stopping work will ever add up. I will not turn in my furnace keys on the strength of a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help you check the figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Celia and I would put written income beside rent, groceries, travel and likely health costs. Our grown children have their own homes; I would not treat their wages as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is only online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the safe paid furnace shift if it remains available. I need a funded supervised place on an isolated machine before I claim an inspection skill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 AGI picture is worst because robots around 2031 could take the furnace crew's physical shifts when we have only two weeks saved. A real funded guarded inspection place accepted locally, written staffing dates and posted safe jobs with enough pay after travel would help. I would keep the paid work until another route is real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who trains the next furnace operator to see a bowed pane. A camera reading is useful only when somebody knows what a bad piece feels like at the straightedge.

headlineQuote: A camera reading is useful only when somebody knows what a bad piece feels like at the straightedge.
portrait: **Ivan**, 58, is a senior glass-furnace shift lead with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional process skill.
He and his **partner Celia** have grown children, a low lead rate, roughly two weeks saved and few similar local plants.
He has **never used AI**, prefers furnace charts and pane checks, and will consider only proven funded safe practical training.
Expected **2031 physical robots** threaten essential wages; any earlier retirement needs verified income covering real household costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 furnace robots** could remove his low-paid lead shift before an adequate local job or affordable retirement is clear.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written staffing dates**, accepted funded guarded inspection training on paid time and real jobs with enough net pay.
